s04.slug: TUESDAY · 3:50 PM · STATE STREET AT CARRILLO — THE SAAB, TOP DOWN
body: February hasn’t reached State Street. The sun is out the length of it, a man in cargo shorts is walking a bulldog in a cable-knit sweater past a store that sells nothing but olive oil, and the palms over the sidewalk stand around in the light like they’re waiting to be tipped. Two hours from Glenwood Avenue a groundhog saw his shadow this morning and ruined six weeks for everybody Jack loves. Out here the Saab’s top is down. It’s been down since Hollis.

She was at the curb when he came out of section, sitting up on the back of the driver’s seat with her sneakers on the cushion and the engine running, vibrating along with it. She didn’t say hello. She said, “I need a coat. I’ve never owned a real coat. You’re from a cold place, you have to come tell me if it’s a coat.” When he had one leg in she said, “I booked it,” and put the car in first, and he got the rest of himself in on the way to the 101.

She told him on the freeway, with the wind taking every third word off the top of her head and throwing it at the oil platforms. He got one thing of his own in somewhere along the water — noon Mass, the candles, a taper at the Mary side for Danny, twenty-three today — and she reached over and squeezed his knee and went straight back to New Mexico. She told him again in the store, from inside a sheepskin coat with a collar you could lose a cat in, walking it up and down in front of the three-way mirror. Now the coat is in a bag on the back seat and they’re at a meter on State with the engine off, and she’s telling him a third time, because as far as he can tell it hasn’t taken on her yet.

“It’s called *Caliche*.” She has both hands on top of the wheel and her chin on her hands. “It’s a kind of dirt. Hard dirt, out in the desert, like a floor somebody poured. It’s cable, it’s an hour, it’s a sheriff in a border town and his daughter, and the daughter’s me, and her name is Dell Harlan.” She sits up. “And she isn’t nice to anybody, Jack. Not one person. She has a horse and she isn’t nice to the horse.”
“Where’s the horse?”

“Outside Santa Fe. Seven thousand feet. It *snows*.” She says it like a word from a language she’s just started taking. “A car comes Saturday at six. Burbank, Albuquerque, and then some van with the show’s name taped in the window. Back the twenty-first.” She counts it off on the wheel, fingers and then fingers again. “Sixteen days.”

He has seen her be Cassidy on Nonna’s television on a Thursday: the good girl, with the hair, who says the right thing in the last two minutes. He has never seen her want anything the way she wants this girl in the snow who isn’t nice to her horse.
“You’re going to scare the hell out of New Mexico,” he says.

“My mother wanted me to pass.” She fishes the Sharpie out of the cup holder and caps it and uncaps it. She does Debbie, one line, the vowels sweet and sharp at once: “*Baby. Cassidy pays for the house.*” And herself again. “The house is paid for. I paid for it. That isn’t what she means.” She puts the key in and doesn’t turn it. “What if I can’t do it? Mean. I’ve never been anybody’s bad news. I don’t know where you keep it.”
“You took it anyway,” Jack says.
“I took it anyway.” She turns the key, and the Saab coughs and catches, and she says it again over the engine, like she wants to hear how it sounds with noise under it.
“Your turn,” she says. “I’ve been talking since Hollis.”

So he tells her about breakfast. The Anchor’s placemats with Theo’s fountain pen all over the tide table; six tickets out of the Delgado lab printer, one with COSTIGAN on it, paid for; the game at the Broussards’, a week of New Orleans, then Bacchus and a quarterback who gets to be king. Ten days. And then Theo putting the pen down and asking him — for himself, he said. Theo doesn’t ask.
“Ted pitched you on a *placemat*.”
“With an act structure.”
“Of course with an act structure.” She doesn’t laugh. She looks out at the street, at the bulldog coming back the other way in its sweater.
“Go,” she says. “Watch your Saints win it in their own city.” A bus goes by, and she waits for it. “Who knows — maybe it’ll be good for you guys.”
He knows what *you guys* is. She has heard four versions of Hale’s seminar from Margot and a fifth from Doug with a dog in it, and she has never asked him for his. She leaves it at *you guys*.
“Friday’s yours,” he says.
“I leave at six on Saturday.”
“I know.”

She takes her sunglasses off and looks at him across the gearshift with nothing in front of her eyes. Then she puts them back on, and puts the Saab in gear, and pulls out onto State without signaling, like a native.

Carrillo is red. Carrillo is always red; the town is built to stop you there. She reaches over and turns the radio up, and the man on the station says something about the weekend, and the song comes on: the slow wet synthesizer, the falsetto, a snare like somebody tapping on the car window with one fingernail. Every Costigan alive would change the station.
“Oh no,” Jack says.
“Oh, *yes*.” She turns it up again. “It’s your brother’s birthday.”
“That’s not what it’s about.”
“I know *exactly* what it’s about.”

She starts it alone, to him, over the gearshift, one finger keeping time on the wheel. He holds out for most of the first verse with his arms folded. The hook comes around and he’s in it with her, at the top of his lungs, both of them, *birthday sex* — on Candlemas, with the noon Mass’s wax still under his thumbnail, at a red light on State Street, eyes on each other.

In the next lane there’s a silver Camry with a girl about Skye’s age at the wheel and a Flip camera held up over her steering wheel, its little red light on, pointed at them. Jack sees it between one line and the next.
“Should she even be *driving* that?” he yells over the chorus. The radio’s been full of Toyotas all week, and somewhere on Glenwood Avenue Frank Costigan is not saying one word about it.
Skye sees the camera. She keeps singing, to Jack. The light stays red. The Flip stays up.

choices.key: At a red light on State Street you and Skye sang “Birthday Sex” at each other, top down, every word. A girl in the next lane filmed it.
response: He knows every word. This is news to both of them. He couldn’t tell you where he learned it — the Delgado laundry room, the showers on four with Pruitt’s radio on the sink, Rudy turning the Anchor’s radio up for this one song and no other — but it’s all in there, the verses, the part where the man explains himself in detail, and he sings every bit of it at her with his hand on his heart and no shame left anywhere in him.

Skye lets go of the wheel to conduct. Both hands, up over the windshield, the sunglasses sliding down her nose. She points at him for the high part, and he goes for it and misses it by a state, and she points again, and he goes again.

The light’s been green a while. He finds this out from the horns: the Camry first, then a bakery van behind them, then what sounds like most of Carrillo. Skye laughs so hard she drops the clutch with no gas, and the Saab bucks once and dies in the crosswalk.
“Clutch,” he says.
“I *know* where the clutch is.”
“In. Now first. Little gas — now ease off —”
“Are you teaching *me* —”
“Ease off. Easy.”

She gets it, and they lurch across Carrillo on the yellow with the song still going and the Camry honking behind them in time, and Jack is grinning at the whole of State Street like a man let out of somewhere early.

choices.text: *Do the backup vocals. All of them.*
choices.key: At a red light on State Street you and Skye sang “Birthday Sex” at each other, top down — you did every backup vocal. A girl in the next lane filmed it.
response: He does the backup vocals. All of them. Every echo under her line, every *yeah*, the little answering *oh* at the back of each bar, the ad-libs nobody has ever sung on purpose, and for the falsetto he can’t hit and never will he puts a hand over his heart and shuts his eyes and tries anyway.

She breaks twice. The first time she folds over the wheel and comes back up and finds her place. The second time she can’t, and he carries the song alone for two lines in a range God did not give him, until she’s back, wiping her eyes under the sunglasses, and takes it from him at the hook.

In the Camry the girl takes one hand off the wheel and gives them a thumbs-up out her window, the Flip steady in the other. The light changes. Skye takes them across Carrillo doing the outro, both parts of it, her elbow up on the door, and Jack does the echoes half a step behind her till the next light.

choices.text: *Sing it to her, not at her.*
choices.key: At a red light on State Street you and Skye sang “Birthday Sex” to each other, top down, eyes on each other the whole time. A girl in the next lane filmed it.
response: He sings it to her. The filthiest song on the radio, and he sings it across the gearshift the way Pop sings Sinatra in the garage when he thinks the house is asleep: slow, a little behind the band, every line a thing he’s handing over. It’s ridiculous. He does it anyway, and he doesn’t look at the Camry once.

Halfway through the second verse she stops laughing. She turns in her seat to face him, one knee up against the gearshift, and sings the next line back to him, and the one after it, at the top of her lungs and straight at him, and in the next lane the girl behind the Flip has gone quiet to watch.

The light goes green, and neither of them notices till the horn behind them, long. She drives across Carrillo one-handed. The other hand is on the back of his neck, and two lights later it hasn’t moved.

s06b.slug: TUESDAY · 8:50 PM · DEL PLAYA LANE, HER ROOM — THE SIDES
body: Every light in her room is on — the lamp, the overhead, the string of Christmas bulbs still tacked over the window — and her iPod is going in its little speaker on the floor by the mattress, the record she’s played all winter. On the mattress is everything she owns that might be warm, in three piles and a fourth pile that’s only socks. In the middle of it sits one suitcase, open, with the look of a suitcase that has just been shown the piles. The coat from State Street hangs on the closet door on the one wooden hanger she owns.

“I said I was bad at it,” Skye says. She’s on her knees in the socks, in leggings and a T-shirt from a 10K she didn’t run, with a pencil stuck through her hair. “I’ve been doing this an hour. So far I’ve packed a hair dryer.”
“They have hair dryers in New Mexico.”
“They have *motels* in New Mexico. I’ve seen pictures.” She holds up a sweater, looks at it, throws it on the third pile. “The pages are on the pillow. You’re the sheriff.”

The pages are on the pillow: her first week, three-hole-punched, folded the long way and gone soft at the fold, DELL down the left margin over and over like a fence, her pencil in every gap. He picks up four of them.
“I’ve never been a sheriff.”
“You’ve never been a lot of things. Read the capitals that say HARLAN. Don’t act. If you act I’ll have to be nice to you.”
He reads the first HARLAN in his own voice, Glenwood Avenue flat. “*Where were you.*”
“No,” Skye says. “He’s fifty. He has a gun he’s never pointed at anybody. He’s been up since yesterday. Do your dad.”

So he does Frank: Frank Costigan at the kitchen door after midnight with the truck keys still in his hand, finding the Silverado a quarter tank lighter than he left it. Low, tired, no question mark on anything.
“*Where were you.*”
And she’s gone. Not far — she’s right there on the mattress, rolling a pair of socks into a ball — but the girl rolling the socks isn’t anybody he’s met. She doesn’t look up. “Out.”
“*Out where.*”
“Out where you can’t find me.” She drops the socks in the suitcase without looking where they land. “Turns out that’s most places.”

He reads the next HARLAN and she’s over the top of it before he’s halfway, which the pages don’t tell her to do, and her eyes come up to him for the first time, and they’ve already decided what he is. She’s dropped her voice half an octave and sped it up, and every word is bored of him, and the back of his neck goes hot.
“*Your mother —*”

“Don’t.” She pulls a sweater off the second pile and folds it perfectly, the first thing she’s folded all night, and lays it in. “You want to talk about Mom, put it in the log, Sheriff. You put everybody else in the log.” She smooths the sweater down. “You found a dead man in an arroyo last spring in forty minutes. In the dark. With one flashlight.” She looks up. “Think about how long you’ve been standing in that door.”
Jack loses his place. It isn’t acting; he can’t find the line. The next HARLAN is somewhere under his thumb, and there’s a girl on the mattress who would let him stand in a doorway till he died.
Then she pulls the pencil out of her hair and her hair comes down, and it’s Skye, cross-legged in a pile of socks, looking at him over the suitcase with her eyebrows up.
“Was that too much?”
“I want to apologize to the horse.”
She laughs and lies back in the socks with the pages on her chest. “*Good*,” she tells the ceiling.
“She’s not mean,” she says, from the socks. “Everybody’s going to say she’s mean. She’s *busy*. Every single thing she says in that kitchen is so he won’t get to the next question.”
“What’s the next question?”

“Who she was with.” She points the pencil straight up. “It isn’t in the pages. Nobody told me. I decided. You have to decide, or you’re just saying the words louder.” She rolls her head on the socks to look at him. “She was with a boy her father put in the back of his car last year. She likes the boy. She knows exactly what her father would do if he knew, and she’s right. So she makes it about her mother, because he’ll let her win anything if it’s about her mother.”
“Augustine stole pears,” Jack says. “Off a tree, with his friends, at sixteen. He didn’t even want them. They threw them to the pigs. He says he did it for nothing — for the wrong of it.”

“He says that. He also says he wouldn’t have done it alone.” She sits up. “You told me that part yourself. He had people watching. People don’t do anything for nothing, Youngstown. He just didn’t like who he was showing off for.”
It’s a better reading than the one he wrote a paper on in eleventh grade, and he tells her so. She writes *PEARS* in the margin of page three and underlines it.
The song on the floor ends and the next one starts. She’s quiet through the first of it, the pages on her knees, her thumb going down the margin from one DELL to the next.
“I don’t know who I am when I’m not the nice one,” she says.
“You’re the one who sang that song at a red light on State Street.”
“That’s not a character.”
“No.”
She sets the pages face down on the suitcase lid and holds out both hands for the socks.

He packs the rest Ma’s way, for a week at the lake: everything rolled tight and stood on end, shoes in the corners stuffed with socks, the hair dryer out. It all goes in, all four piles, with room left over. Skye watches from the pillow with her chin on her knees and her eyes on his hands. The coat she keeps out. She’s wearing it on the plane.

At the front door she kisses him in it, over the 10K shirt, with the big collar turned up around her ears because, she says, she wants to know what it’s like to be cold in it, and it’s fifty-five degrees on the porch. Down the bluff stairs the surf is loud.
“Goodnight, Sheriff.”
“Goodnight, Dell.”
“No,” Skye says, with her hand on the door. “The other one.”
“Goodnight, Misfit.”
She pulls the collar up over her mouth, and over it her eyes are all hers.

s15.slug: THURSDAY · 3:40 PM · CAMPUS POINT LOT — THE SAAB, DANNY’S LETTER

journal.title: Danny Costigan
journal.text: My brother. Trumbull Correctional. Calls me Professor. Ma brought him the good socks. *Brideshead* went to him through Driftwood, margins erased; the C.O. reading it first says it’s about a house. The ocean letter got there; Reggie, from Portsmouth, decided on his own the Pacific smells like money and fish. Lena knows. She asked his name. On the bluff bench she said hi to him and told him she’s going to be defense, and he laughed like he used to. The system cut him off at ‘tell Gina — .’ He wrote the rest down: tell Gina it ain’t hers to carry. He’s got it. On Michaelmas he wrote: Tell Lena hey. I like knowing it. You sound happy out there. Don’t feel bad about it. That’s an order. Lena says hey back. She said it herself. The Saints are four and oh, and she expects him to know that. Third letter, after Columbus Day: the Hopkins got there. He read Ma “Felix Randal” on the phone and she cried; he says he’s telling me so I know he read it, not so I feel bad. The Housman made Reggie cry. Ma told him about Becca. He wants to know if I told Lena hey, or does he have to come out here. I did. He doesn’t know yet. Push-ups: 140. Fourth letter, All Souls: he knows about hey now. ABOUT TIME, up the margin; he wants to know what she said back. Halloween at Trumbull, a guard in a rubber mask. Ma’s getting Nonno a Mass at St. Brigid’s; he wants me to put Nonno in the book here. He says he’d put his in, but he doesn’t have anybody dead. He has the other kind. I wrote him back: she said hey like she meant it. Thanksgiving weekend: put in for a visit for the rich one himself. Liked him in a minute. Reggie waved. Asked which girl. ‘Who’s Flannery O’Connor?’ Noticed I waited till Theo went to the machines. Told Theo he could quit buying. He went to the prison library about Flannery O’Connor. Ma read it to me off an envelope: she raised peacocks and she was mean and he likes her. Is it still something. The Sunday before Christmas I went with Ma; Pop stayed in the truck — the twenty-seventh, he says. Ma took forever at the machines. He said it for me — I’m in love with Lena — and I didn’t tell him he was wrong. Then the rest: the song, the month, Skye. He said he wasn’t going to tell me which one. He said he believes me, both. Then he asked me one question, and I didn’t have an answer. Then he told Ma I miss the beach. Christmas Eve I brought Theo, in the parka. Theo bought; Danny let him. Theo asked if I’d told him about California. Danny said I miss the beach. Asked Theo who comes to see him. “He does.” Christmas, Gina told him about the boat, and he laughed till they cut him off in the middle of a sentence about Lena. Holy Family Sunday, all of us — Pop too. He stood up when he saw Pop. Pop told him they wouldn’t lose. Laughed at the TV one till the guard looked over. Paddle boats: she’s not to know. Asked the table her name, like he didn’t have it. While Ma showed Pop the machines he asked me not to let Pop sit in the truck on the third. Asked Pop about the hall; says the Cruze sounds like a boat. Pop brought him coffee with cream and sugar. He drinks it black. He drank it. Epiphany Sunday, Maria’s Sunday: Pop went in again. Danny stood up. Pop told him the Browns would win, and they did — four straight. Then a letter, in capitals: IS SHE BLIND OR DID YOU LIE. Gina’s yacht got to Trumbull. Sunday, Ma’s Sunday, Gina told him her name across the table at Trumbull and described the taco picture. He said *a NUN?* He said ask her what she lost the bet for. He laughed so hard the CO came over. Ma said happy birthday early in case my card’s late. He said late’s a Costigan tradition. Candlemas he turned twenty-three. The unit let him call on a Tuesday, for his birthday, and he spent it on me. The block sang. I told him Theo asked me to New Orleans and I said no. He asked was it because of the TV one or the veil girl. I said neither. He said that’s two. Thursday his letter to Skye came in my box, in capitals, his number in the corner. She read it to me in the Saab. I sing like a goat at a funeral. I’ll tell the truth even when it costs me; that’s the whole trouble with me.

body: The wind has come around off the water since lunch, and it has teeth in it for the first time in weeks. The Campus Point lot is down to surfboards and Subarus and a girl changing under a beach towel with her elbows out. The Saab is nosed up to the rail at the far end with the top up for once and the radio off, and out past the point the islands have gone under a low gray lid.
His flannel from the Walk is on the back seat, folded on top of a Ralphs bag of things she forgot to pack Tuesday. She reaches back for it blind.

“This is coming with me,” she says. “It went to San Francisco. It can go to Santa Fe.” She puts it on over her T-shirt and buttons it to the throat, the sleeves down past her hands, and then goes into the Ralphs bag again and comes out with a gray sweatshirt and drops it in his lap. SWEETWATER ACADEMY CREW. “You get this. It’s the only honest thing I own.”
“For how long?”
“Sixteen days.” She points at it. “Washed.”
“By who?”
“By you. In the Delgado laundry room. I’ll know.”

He holds it up. The cuffs are chewed, both of them, and it smells like the Saab’s heater and whatever she puts in her hair. Her iPhone buzzes in the cup holder. She reads it off the screen in Corinne’s vowels — “*Thursday is a new day*” — and drops the phone in the Ralphs bag with the things she forgot, and folds the top of the bag over it.
He gives her the envelope. It’s been in the inside pocket of the Carhartt since the mailboxes this morning, Danny’s capitals marching across the front of it to her name.
“He said don’t read it,” Jack says. “I didn’t.”
“You held it up to a light.”
“Once.”
She opens it with a thumb under the flap, slowly, and takes out one sheet of lined paper written to the edges, and smooths it on the steering wheel, and reads it to him.

body.title: TRUMBULL CORRECTIONAL INSTITUTION
body.text:
MISS SKYE,
Thank you for writing me. Nobody writes me but the Professor and Gina and Gina writes in colors.
You wrote my number bigger than the State of Ohio does. The CO read it out at mail call like a ballgame. I am famous on the range now. Reggie wants to know are you the girl on the yacht. I told him a lady don’t answer that.
Gina says you’re on TV Thursdays. We got one TV in the dayroom and it’s whatever the loudest guy wants, and the loudest guy wants wrestling. I’m working on him.
My brother sings like a goat at a funeral. If he ever sings to you, I’m sorry. I’m sorry ahead of time.
He’ll tell you the truth even when it costs him. That’s the whole trouble with him.
Write me back if you want. You don’t got to.
Push-ups 170.
DANNY
A555218

body: At Reggie she stops. “Who’s Reggie?”
“Portsmouth. He was Balthazar at Epiphany. The myrrh was a honey bun.”

“I love Reggie,” she says, and goes on. She gets as far as the goat and no farther. She puts her forehead down on the steering wheel and laughs into the horn ring, and the horn doesn’t go off, and that sets her off again, and she has to sit up and wipe her eyes on the cuff of his flannel before she can find her place.
“He wrote this *last week*,” she says.
“He’s been in a car with me.”

She reads the rest. *He’ll tell you the truth even when it costs him* she reads exactly as it’s written, no faster and no slower, and looks over at him across the gearshift before she goes on. There’s a sentence like that in every letter Danny sends. Jack watches the gray water out past the rail until she’s by it.
“*Push-ups one-seventy*,” she finishes.
It was a hundred and forty at Columbus Day.
She folds the letter along its old fold and holds it in her lap in both hands. “I’m writing him from New Mexico,” she says. “What can you send? To there.”
“Letters. Books — softcover, no staples. Theo called and asked. Photographs, regular ones. No Polaroids.”
“Why no Polaroids?”
“You can hide things in them. Between the layers.”
“Like what?”
“Ask Danny.”

She takes Dell’s pages off the dash and the Sharpie out of the cup holder and writes a list down the margin of the back page in capitals, as if capitals are the house style now: LETTERS. BOOKS — SOFT — NO STAPLES. PHOTOS (NOT POLAROID). Under it, after a minute, she adds WRESTLING?? and taps it twice with the cap.
“Would he want a picture?”
“Of you?”
“Of the horse. Dell’s horse. I’m going to make friends with it on my own time, so she doesn’t have to.” She writes HORSE under WRESTLING. “Would he put it up?”
“Where Reggie can see it,” Jack says. “Every day. Till Reggie’s sick of it.”
“Good,” she says, and underlines HORSE.

choices.key: Skye read Danny’s letter aloud in the Saab. You told her he’s right about the goat.
response: “I was *there*, Youngstown. He’s being generous.”

And she does the goat. She does it at a funeral, with grief, with dignity, with the high part, her head back against the seat and one hand over her heart, and it’s him, it’s exactly him at Carrillo, and a surfer coming up from the beach stairs with his board under his arm stops beside the Saab to look in.
She starts the car doing it. Jack, who has given up, sits there with the sweatshirt in his lap, grinning at her like an idiot, while she does a second verse for the surfer.
“Is she okay?” the surfer asks Jack.
“She’s at a funeral,” Jack says, and Skye puts the Saab in reverse without breaking character, mourning, out of the space.

choices.text: “Write him back. He’ll read it forty times.”
choices.key: Skye read Danny’s letter aloud in the Saab. You told her to write him back — he’ll read it forty times.
response: “Forty,” she says. She looks at the capitals. “Then I’ll write small. Make him work for it.”
“He reads mine out to Reggie. Reggie’s got a theory about the Pacific now. Money and fish.”

She writes DANNY — FROM NEW MEXICO at the top of the list, over the books, and draws a box around it, the way Gina boxed *yacht* in a letter Skye has never seen. She slides his letter in between Dell’s pages at the very front, where the first day goes, and closes the pages on it.

choices.key: Skye read Danny’s letter aloud in the Saab. You told her he means it about the truth.
response: “I know,” she says. “That’s why I wrote him.” She turns the Sharpie end over end on her knee. “I wrote him three times, the first time. I threw two away. They were in a voice.”

She looks down at the capitals in her lap. “Everybody who writes me writes in a voice. Corinne’s, my mother’s, the network’s. Your brother writes like he’s standing in front of me with his hands in his pockets.”
She starts the Saab and lets it idle at the rail, the heater coming up and the wind rocking the canvas top, and only when the vents have gone warm does she put it in gear.
